analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage to $4.25 over three years, with offsets for small businesses and tipped workers.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have raised the minimum wage from $3.35 to $4.25 an hour over three years, was sent to a House subcommittee in April 1989 and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would raise the federal minimum wage in three steps, from $3.35 to $3.65 in 1990, $3.95 in 1991, and $4.25 in 1992 and after. To offset employer costs, it would also let restaurants count more tips toward the minimum wage, exempt more small firms from coverage, and let employers pay brand-new hires a lower rate for up to 180 days. It was referred to a House subcommittee and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers paid the federal minimum wage would get raises in three annual steps to $4.25 an hour by 1992, a 27% increase over the $3.35 rate in effect since 1981. The benefit is uneven: tipped workers could legally be paid as little as half the minimum in direct wages because the tip credit rises to 50%, workers at newly exempted small businesses would be stuck at $3.35 or lose coverage, and brand-new hires could be paid the old $3.35 rate for up to 180 days.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the federal minimum wage in three steps to $3.65 in 1990, $3.95 in 1991, and $4.25 in 1992 and thereafter, up from $3.35.
Preserves a $3.35 hourly floor for workers at businesses that lose coverage under the new, higher $500,000 small-business exemption, so they do not fall below the wage they were already owed.
Bars employers from displacing existing workers — including by cutting hours or benefits — to replace them with cheaper new hires paid the lower training rate.

analysis.who_pays: Employers covered by the Fair Labor Standards Act — businesses with annual sales above $500,000, including retail, service, and restaurant chains — would bear the higher wage bill. Restaurant owners would recoup part of it through the larger tip credit, and firms below the $500,000 threshold would be exempted from coverage altogether.
analysis.who_pays_short: Covered employers, mainly retail and restaurant chains

drawbacks.text: Raises the tip credit from 40% to 50%, letting employers count half the minimum wage as coming from customers' tips — so tipped employees could legally take home as little as half the minimum wage in direct pay, and the CRS summary describes a 45% step in 1990 before 50%.

Expands the small-business exemption from $362,500 to $500,000 in annual gross sales, removing minimum wage and overtime protection from some workers entirely; newly exempted employers would still owe $3.35, but their workers would miss the future increases.

Creates a subminimum starting wage: employers could pay brand-new hires $3.35 an hour — later 80% of the minimum — for up to 180 days, weakening the raise for people starting a job, though with anti-displacement protections.
The full $4.25 rate would not arrive until 1992, three years after introduction, leaving the real value of $3.35 to erode further in the meantime.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: This is a genuine minimum wage increase, but a deliberately diluted one: every dollar of the raise is partly clawed back through a larger tip credit, a broader small-business exemption, and a 180-day subminimum for new hires. Minimum wage workers come out ahead overall, tipped workers and new hires gain the least, and workers at newly exempted small businesses could be locked out of future increases. It reads as a compromise package designed to be harder for business opponents to fight, and it still never got a vote.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee and then to its Labor Standards subcommittee, where it sat without a hearing or vote until the 101st Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative William Goodling, a Pennsylvania Republican, introduced the bill on March 14, 1989 with nine other original cosponsors from both parties.
The House referred it to the Committee on Education and Labor the same day it was introduced.
On April 5, 1989, the committee sent it to its Subcommittee on Labor Standards — the last action ever recorded on the bill.
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote appears in the action history for the rest of the 101st Congress, which ended January 3, 1991.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Covered employers were better off because the bill never moved, since it carried a wage increase they avoided (though by general historical record, Congress passed a different minimum wage increase later in 1989, so low-wage workers did not go without a raise that year). The committee and subcommittee that buried it kept control over which minimum wage package, if any, would advance.

for.name: Rep. William Goodling
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on March 14, 1989 with nine other original cosponsors, pairing a minimum wage increase with offsets for small business and tipped employers.

for.name: 9 of 175 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the majority of its 12 cosponsors.

against.name: House Education and Labor Committee
against.what_they_did: Took the referral on March 14, 1989 and sent the bill to subcommittee; never held a markup or moved it to the floor.

against.name: Subcommittee on Labor Standards, House Education and Labor
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on April 5, 1989 and took no further action on it for the remainder of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's 12 cosponsors split 9 Republicans and 3 Democrats with a Republican lead sponsor, but it never reached a floor vote, so no vote split exists to measure.

industries.industry: Restaurants and other employers of tipped workers
industries.note: The bill raises their labor costs through the higher minimum wage but hands them a larger tip credit (40% to 50%), letting them pay tipped staff as little as half the minimum in direct wages, plus a cheaper 180-day rate for new hires. Tipped workers, who are mostly ordinary wage earners, give up part of the raise in exchange.

industries.industry: Small businesses under $500,000 in annual sales
industries.note: The exemption threshold rises from $362,500 to $500,000, removing these employers from minimum wage and overtime coverage entirely; their gain comes at the cost of their workers' protection, though firms already covered in 1988 must still pay $3.35.

industries.industry: Retail and service chains above the coverage threshold
industries.note: These covered employers would pay the full phased increase to $4.25 by 1992, with only the new-hire subminimum as partial relief.
